draft.title: Identity and inverse matrices
card: The identity matrix I is a square matrix with 1s down the main diagonal and 0s elsewhere. For any matrix A of a matching order, A × I = A and I × A = A.
The inverse of A is written A⁻¹. It is the matrix where A × A⁻¹ = I. Only a square matrix can have an inverse, and not every square matrix has one.
For A = [a b; c d], the determinant is ad − bc. If it is 0, there is no inverse. If not, A⁻¹ = 1/(ad − bc) × [d −b; −c a].
draft.remember: A matrix times its inverse gives I. No inverse if the determinant is 0.

a.q: What is the determinant of the matrix [4 3; 2 5]?
a.why: The determinant is ad − bc = 4×5 − 3×2 = 20 − 6 = 14. The value 26 comes from adding the products instead of subtracting them.
a.clue: Multiply the main diagonal, then take away the other diagonal's product.

b.q: For which value of k does the matrix [2 k; 3 6] have no inverse?
b.why: The determinant is 2×6 − k×3 = 12 − 3k. It equals 0 when k = 4, so there is no inverse. When k = 0 the determinant is 12, which is not 0, so an inverse exists.
b.clue: Set the determinant equal to 0 and solve for k.

problems.detail: 'For any matrix A of a matching order, A × I = A and I × A = A' suggests one identity matrix works on both sides of any A. For a non-square A (m × n), A × I needs the n × n identity and I × A needs the m × m identity. It would be clearer to say the identity used must match the side it multiplies on, or to limit this statement to square A.

check.summary: The facts, the worked example and both answers are correct (det = 14; no inverse when k = 4). There is one minor wording issue: the identity line implies a single I works on both sides of a non-square matrix.

final.title: Identity and inverse matrices
card: The identity matrix \(I\) is a square matrix with 1s down the main diagonal and 0s elsewhere. For a square matrix \(A\), using \(I\) of the same order, \(A \times I = A\) and \(I \times A = A\).
The inverse of \(A\) is written \(A^{-1}\). It is the matrix where \(A \times A^{-1} = I\). Only a square matrix can have an inverse, and not every square matrix has one.

For \(A = \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix}\), the determinant is \(ad - bc\). If it is 0, there is no inverse. If not, \(A^{-1} = \frac{1}{ad - bc} \times \begin{bmatrix} d & -b \\ -c & a \end{bmatrix}\).
final.remember: A matrix times its inverse gives \(I\). No inverse if the determinant is 0.

a.q: What is the determinant of the matrix \(\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 3 \\ 2 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\)?
a.why: The determinant is \(ad - bc = 4 \times 5 - 3 \times 2\), which is \(20 - 6 = 14\). The value 26 comes from adding the products instead of subtracting them.
a.clue: Multiply the main diagonal, then take away the other diagonal's product.

b.q: For which value of \(k\) does the matrix \(\begin{bmatrix} 2 & k \\ 3 & 6 \end{bmatrix}\) have no inverse?
b.why: The determinant is \(2 \times 6 - k \times 3 = 12 - 3k\). It equals 0 when \(k = 4\), so there is no inverse. When \(k = 0\) the determinant is 12, which is not 0, so an inverse exists.
b.clue: Set the determinant equal to 0 and solve for \(k\).
